Common parent framework: US. Parent rating given: 0.35. The parent framework includes: passport sex-marker restrictions (X markers discontinued, marker must match birth sex for new applications), entry screening with case-note tags, potential fraud/ lifetime ineligibility findings, trans athlete entry ban, detention/custody harm (conversion-therapy-like policies, denial of care, abuse in immigration custody), facility bans in many states, etc. But also: no national sodomy law, hate-crime statute covering gender identity nationally, employment discrimination prohibited nationally, marriage equality.

Parent rating 0.35 = High Risk band (0.20–0.40).

Now each division:

Dossier 1: New Jersey. Strong state-level protections: anti-discrimination covering gender identity in public accommodations, hotels, lodging, with an enforcement body; bias-crime enhancements; birth-certificate change without surgery since 2019; X markers; shield law (April 2023 EO protecting gender-affirming care including for people traveling in); panic defence barred; sodomy repealed; Most Protective tier; among safest per capita rates of trans killings. Best-documented division. Should be highest, in Reduced Risk / near Low Risk. Given the parent's border/entry exposure still applies (passport/visa national rules), it can't be too high. State-level: strong accommodations protections, hotels/restaurants covered, enforcement body. Violence: safest measured per-capita.

I'd put Dossier 1 around 0.62–0.68. The national entry exposure is universal for all five dossiers, so divisions differ by local layer. Since the parent is 0.35 and this adds strong protections and documented low violence, but the national regime still governs border/entry and federal facilities/custody... Actually rule 12 about dependent territories applies to territories, not states — but here all states are under the same national framework, so the national exposure applies equally. The question: how much can a state layer move above the parent? The rubric says the division's rating should reflect the mean local regime in addition to the national picture. A protective state with documented protections actually operating (accommodations anti-discrimination with enforcement body, shield law, low violence) sits well above the national line. But the entry/border exposure is universal and outranks.

Let me calibrate. Parent 0.35 = High Risk. For Dossier 1, local regime strongly protective with documented enforcement machinery; the traveller-facing exposure is mainly the national border/document issue (which applies to all). I'd rate 0.60–0.65.

Hmm, but the border exposure is severe: passports confiscated, entry screening, lifetime ineligibility risk, trans athletes barred. That's the same for all. Actually wait — the trans athlete ban and visa fraud risk apply to visitors nationally. For a trans visitor, entry is the sharpest exposure. That caps everything. So even the best state can't exceed maybe 0.65-0.70 because the entry experience is national.

Dossier 2: Low-risk group of nine — "largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection." Anti-discrimination since 2013 covering employment, housing, public accommodations; hate-crime enhancements; no bathroom ban; panic defence bill passed but governor didn't sign; state ID marker change on provider statement; no X marker; but core protections predate current posture. This is a moderately protective state — weaker than 1 (no explicit facilitiy protection law? actually no bathroom ban, and accommodations discrimination ban covers services). No documented violence data. I'd put around 0.50–0.55.

Dossier 3: Most Protective tier, shield law 2022 for visitors from ban states, anti-discrimination public places/services/employment since 2011, hate crime covering GI strengthened 2026, X markers, custody treatment consistent with gender identity (2018 policy — this is interesting; custody placement by gender identity is traveller-facing if detained, positive), panic defence repealed, youth care protections. Strong. Similar to 1, maybe slightly below 1 because 1 has documented lowest violence rate and accommodation-enforcement body. Actually 1 has documented low trans-killing rate which is strong positive evidence; 3 has no violence data (silent — in a well-documented state, silence is mildly positive). I'd put 1 slightly above 3: 1 = 0.63, 3 = 0.60.

Hmm, but 3 has the shield law explicitly relevant to visitors, plus in-custody treatment by gender identity (a direct protection for a detained traveller — that's important given the custody exposure). 3 also has anti-discrimination covering public places. 1 has accommodations enforcement body plus hotel/lodging explicitly covered and documented low violence. I'll give 1 = 0.63, 3 = 0.60.

Dossier 4: Also Most Protective tier; GENDA 2019 covering credit, housing, employment, education, public accommodations; hate crime covering GI; constitutional amendment 2024; X markers widely; shield law 2023 including barring law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-jurisdiction agencies; repealed the loitering statute used to harass trans people; gender-neutral bathroom mandate; conversion therapy ban; huge trans population, LGBTQ-general tolerance polling (75%→82% support for discrimination protections; note LGBTQ-general). No trans-specific violence data. Very similar to 3, arguably a bit stronger in shield scope. I'd give 0.61.

Dossier 5: Arkansas. SAFE Act banning youth care; Medicaid ban; prison care ban (no taper); sports ban; birth certificate change requires surgery (with 2013 exceptions reversed 2022); driver's licence gender marker reverted to requiring surgery/court order; no gender-identity non-discrimination law; tipline for reporting care-ban violations; hate crime covers gender identity (but that's weak). Two cities as sanctuaries. This is the weakest. Note: much of this is resident-facing (youth care ban, Medicaid, marker change). But the marker-change surgical requirement... does it reach visitors? Visitors carry home-issued documents; state ID rules are resident-facing. However, the custody/facility exposure: prison care ban (no taper) — an arrested traveller would face denial of HRT and placement questions. Also, state facilities: bathroom access not banned here (no such law), but no protections. The tipline is hostility signal. Also the state is in the "no protections" group.

The state's hostility raising discovery-risk? Not much. But resident-facing gaps don't count against the traveller per rule 1. So for Dossier 5: state has no anti-discrimination protections (resident gap, lightest weight), no bathroom ban (positive-ish), no documented trans violence, hate crime statute covers GI. Downside: hostile state posture, care ban in custody (traveller-relevant if detained), tipline creating hostile reporting environment, restored surgical requirement for markers (resident-facing but signals hostility), no protections for travellers.

Where does it land relative to parent 0.35? Its own layer adds hostility: prison care denial (tier 1 for a detained traveller — "restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres" plus HB 2009 no taper) — that's custody care denial, tier 1-ish. And no non-discrimination protections, so a trans visitor facing service refusal in a hotel has no recourse. Hmm, but national law (2020 Bostock) covers employment, and there's a national hate-crime statute covering gender identity — those are national.

So Dossier 5 sits materially below the protective states and probably below the parent average of 0.35. Given 4 states flagged Do Not Travel and the parent rating 0.35 includes all states. A state with active hostile measures (care ban including in custody, tipline, no protections) should be maybe 0.28–0.32.

I'll say 5 = 0.30.

Let me reconsider the whole spread. Five dossiers: 4 protective (1,3,4 strongly; 2 moderately), 1 hostile (5).

Scores:
1: 0.63
2: 0.52
3: 0.61
4: 0.62
5: 0.30

Hmm, is 0.52 right for 2? Dossier 2: Low-Risk group, no bathroom ban, 2013 anti-discrimination covering accommodations, hate-crime enhancements, no X marker, panic defence bill unsigned/unclear. That's a decent state layer, but no explicit positive documents/protections like shield laws. Compared to 3/4 which have shield laws and X markers and constitutional amendments. 2 sits a step below. 0.52 sounds reasonable given the national entry exposure caps everything.

Actually, should protective states be higher, like 0.65-0.70? The national entry exposure is quite severe: passports confiscated, refusal, lifetime ineligibility, entry screening. That's a tier-1 universal exposure reaching every trans visitor regardless of state. So the ceiling for even the best state should be meaningfully below 0.80. Given that, 0.63 seems reasonable, maybe 0.65.

Let me keep: 1=0.63, 4=0.62, 3=0.61, 2=0.52, 5=0.30.

Hmm, ordering 3 vs 4: 3 has explicit shield law 2022 relevant to visitors, in-custody treatment by gender identity (2018), X markers, hate crime strengthened effective Oct 2026. 4 has broader GENDA, constitutional amendment, shield 2023 broader (barring LE cooperation), bathroom mandate, repealed loitering statute. Roughly equal. I'll put 4 marginally above 3 by 0.01 for the broader shield and loitering repeal, or keep equal. Rule: don't force difference. I'll give 3=0.61, 4=0.62.
